title: Planispheric astrolabe, Iran, 1654–55
summary: A brass astrolabe from Safavid Iran. Its rotating star map (the rete) carries pointers named after real stars, many still known by their Arabic names today, such as Aldebaran (al-Dabaran) and Vega (al-Waqi). Turned against the sky, it tells the time, the height of the sun and the hours of prayer.
creator: Muhammad Zaman al-Munajjim al-Asturlabi
source_name: The Met, Department of Islamic Art (Open Access)

title: Horary quadrant, 10th century
summary: A quarter-circle instrument: sight the sun along its edge and a plumb line falls across curved hour lines. Muwaqqits (mosque timekeepers) used quadrants like this to find the hours of the day and the times of prayer.
creator: Muhammad ibn Mahmud
source_name: The Met, Department of Islamic Art (Open Access)

title: Book of the Images of the Fixed Stars, late 15th century
summary: A copy of ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sufi’s Book of Fixed Stars (written in Isfahan around 964). Al-Sufi drew each constellation twice, as seen on a globe and as seen in the sky, and corrected Ptolemy’s star positions and brightnesses by his own observation.
creator: `Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi
source_name: The Met, Department of Islamic Art (Open Access)

title: Book of the Fixed Stars, 18th-century copy
summary: Eight centuries after al-Sufi, copyists were still drawing his star figures. His book records the earliest known description of the Andromeda Galaxy, the “little cloud”, and it kept Arabic star names alive in astronomy.
creator: `Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi
source_name: The Met, Department of Islamic Art (Open Access)

title: Ulugh Beg, the astronomer-ruler
summary: A modern statue of Mirza Ulugh Beg in Samarkand. He governed the city but is remembered for the sky: his star tables were copied across the Muslim world and translated in Oxford two centuries later.

title: The Maragha observatory, Iran
summary: The domed shelter over the foundations of the observatory founded in 1259 at Maragha by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. Its library and instruments drew astronomers from as far as China, and its planetary models later reappear in Copernicus.

title: Al-Tusi and his colleagues at Maragha
summary: A Persian miniature of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi with fellow astronomers and their instruments at the Maragha observatory. Al-Tusi’s “couple”, two circles rolling inside each other, turned circular motion into straight-line motion.

title: Taqi al-Din’s observatory, Istanbul, 1577
summary: A miniature from the Shahinshahnama showing Taqi al-Din and his team in the Istanbul observatory: astronomers with an astrolabe, a globe, a mechanical clock and books. Taqi al-Din used clocks to time star positions, a new idea at the time.

title: A sine quadrant (rubʿ) on display in Istanbul
summary: A rubʿ al-mujayyab, the sine quadrant. Its grid of lines let a timekeeper solve spherical trigonometry by sliding a thread, without writing a single sum: the hour, the qibla, the height of the sun.

title: Al-Sufi’s star figures
summary: A page from a copy of al-Sufi’s Book of Fixed Stars. Each figure carries red dots for its stars, with their Arabic names written beside them.

title: A zij explained: Kashf Haqaʾiq Zij-i Ilkhani
summary: A zij is a book of astronomical tables. This is al-Nishaburi’s commentary on the Ilkhani Zij, the tables made at Maragha, copied in Timurid Iran in 1432. Tables like these gave the positions of the sun, moon and planets for any date.

title: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur, and the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi
summary: Sawai Jai Singh built these stone instruments in the 1720s–30s and dedicated his star tables, the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi, to the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah. They were modelled on Ulugh Beg’s Samarkand tables.

title: Dar al-Muwaqqit, the timekeeper’s room, Fez
summary: The timekeeping room of the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez, where the muwaqqit kept water clocks and instruments to set the call to prayer. The muwaqqit was a salaried scientific post at the mosque.

title: A muvakkithane, Istanbul
summary: A small timekeeper’s house in a mosque courtyard in Istanbul. Ottoman cities had dozens of these. The muvakkit inside checked the sun and set the clocks for the five prayers.

title: Mustafa ibn ʿAli al-Muwaqqit
summary: A page by Mustafa ibn ʿAli (d. 1571), timekeeper of the Selimiye mosque complex in Istanbul. He wrote Turkish handbooks on instruments, timekeeping and finding the qibla, so working muwaqqits could use them.

title: Al-Battani on the phases of the moon
summary: A page from a printed edition of al-Battani’s great zij, written in Raqqa around 900. Al-Battani refined the length of the solar year and the tilt of the earth’s axis, and was still being cited by astronomers seven centuries later.

title: Astrolabe in an Iranian collection
summary: An Iranian brass astrolabe with its engraved plates for different latitudes. Swapping the plate let the same instrument work in another city.

title: Persian astrolabe, 18th century
summary: The back of a Persian astrolabe, with scales for the sun’s height and a shadow square for measuring the height of buildings and mountains.

title: The new crescent that opens Ramadan

title: The Eid crescent from Pune
